stories.title: Prepare for supply chain disruption from cyber or climate emergencies, Streeting warns
stories.summary: The defence secretary says the UK needs to be ready for scenarios including impact to essential supply chains.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 22 October 2026

Members of the public and businesses need to think more about how they would cope with natural disasters, cyber-attacks or state-sponsored terrorism, the defence secretary has said.

Wes Streeting warned people needed to be more aware of emerging risks facing the UK and make plans to deal with them.

He added that the government was launching a "national resilience conversation" to raise awareness, including advice for households like stocking up on food, bottled water and first aid supplies.

Streeting also said that cyber incidents - like the recently discovered critical security flaw in the programming language which powers much of the internet - will happen "more and more".

Streeting told BBC One's Question Time that the UK is facing a greater threat to the country, "than we have certainly for most, if not all, of my lifetime".

Speaking to an audience at the UK Gun Hall Plant in Telford earlier on Thursday, where it was announced production of tank gun barrels would return to the UK, he spoke of "everyday challenges" facing households.

He pointed to wildfires burning this summer and the flooding that is expected this winter.

Streeting said the public need to be prepared for "increasingly sophisticated cyber-attacks" on businesses, or supply chain disruption caused by "hostile state actors or terrorists".

The defence secretary referenced the critical security flaw in the PHP programming language which has left organisations around the world scrambling to update their systems.

In the UK, 32 government services were offline while the potential cyber-security issues were addressed.

"It's not just from foreign states engaged in espionage or sabotage; it's also organised criminals," Streeting told Question Time.

"In this world of AI that we live in... it does also present threats if people are innovating and pushing against conventional [cyber] defences."

Burnham suggests stocking up on tinned food and bottled water Published 7 hours ago

Why should I stockpile and what will I need? Published 6 hours ago

The government hopes to improve the UK's preparedness for emergencies, such as those caused by increasingly likely severe weather events and cyber-attacks by hostile states.

Incidents could leave the public without access to everyday services such as mains water, sewage, phones and the internet.

The "Be Ready" campaign , external encourages households to stock up on supplies to survive for three days, including non-perishable food, bottled water, a torch, sleeping bags, and first aid items.

It also suggests having a FM radio for updates during outages, and writing down the frequencies of any national or local radio stations you use for news.

Asked by a Question Time audience member whether the campaign amounted to scaremongering, Streeting said the government want "people to be alert but not alarmed".

He said that there was not a "specific thing we've got in mind" when putting out the advice.

But, he added that the supplies on the list "might help you through some power cuts, or might also help you through if... your local shop's subject to a cyber-attack and your card isn't working at the till".

Security Minister Dan Jarvis MP said the advice will ensure emergency services can prioritise people who need more support during crises, and hopes it will "improve our resilience as a nation".

The defence secretary on Thursday spoke at the opening of the UK Gun Hall Plant in Telford, Shropshire

It follows on from similar campaigns by European countries, like France, Ireland and the Netherlands, where the advice is a "normal part of everyday life", he added.

Last month Environment Secretary Dame Angela Eagle said people should prepare for extreme weather as the strongest El Niño event in a generation develops over the Pacific Ocean.

She said the powerful natural climate phenomenon will lead to "more extreme storms in this country", and that households should stock up on food to be more resilient.

Her comments came as an National Audit Office (NAO) report warned Britain's food supply chain is vulnerable to plant or human disease outbreaks, cyber-attacks and extreme weather.

The NAO said the Department for Food, the Environment and Rural Affairs (Defra) had not done enough in recent years to improve supply chain resilience, and that UK households are less prepared for emergencies than those in several other countries such as Finland and Sweden.

The government launched its national security strategy last year, which warned that the UK must "actively prepare for the possibility of the UK coming under direct threat, potentially in a wartime scenario".

It said the nation was "in an era in which we face confrontation with those who are threatening security", and referred to Russia's war against Ukraine and "Iranian hostile activity on British soil".

The government said building national resilience meant reducing reliance on others and ensuring UK supply chains and energy security could be maintained "even in times of crisis".

stories.title: Council vows support for Toxic Town public inquiry
stories.summary: Martin Griffiths, Reform UK leader of North Northants Council, says: "We have nothing to hide."
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
The steelworks in Corby, pictured, closed in 1981

Published 22 October 2026

A council leader says he will support a public inquiry into contaminated land in a town, following a report published last week that revealed it could pose a risk to human health.

The charity Earthwatch Europe says trained citizen scientists have found potentially harmful levels of metal or metalloid at 52 freshwater sites across Corby.

Children in Corby have been born with birth defects, believed to have been caused when steelworks were demolished in the 1980s.

As first reported in the NN Journal, Martin Griffiths, Reform UK leader of North Northamptonshire Council said: "We have nothing to hide."

He added: "We would welcome a genuinely independent examination of the historic events and the questions that remain unanswered, and we would cooperate fully with any inquiry established by the government."

Griffiths challenged the Labour MP for Corby and East Northamptonshire, Lee Barron, to take his longstanding calls for a public inquiry directly to the Labour government.

In response, Barron said it was "baffling" the council would ask for a public inquiry.

He said the authority needed to immediately publish a plan to investigate and clean up any contaminated land.

Barron said: "It is important that North Northamptonshire Council investigates the [Earthwatch] report.

"People deserve answers and it is the role of the council to provide them."

Earthwatch Europe said volunteers found the chemical element cadmium in six freshwater samples in July

Earlier this week, Barron wrote to both the leader of North Northamptonshire Council and the Health Secretary Yvette Cooper.

In his letters, seen by the BBC, he said the findings from the environmental charity "need to be investigated as a matter of urgency".

He has also called on the health secretary to "ensure North Northamptonshire Council take immediate action to clean up any contaminated land".

Parents are calling for more transparency around issues they believe are causing illnesses

Earlier this year, a number of families gathered outside North Northamptonshire's Corby headquarters calling for a public inquiry to clarify the situation.

Des Collins, the solicitor who represented families affected by the town's toxic waste scandal, said: "We welcome the leader's announcement, which finally admits what we have been telling his council for the past year - our clients need, and deserve, a public inquiry as it is the only feasible way of getting to the truth behind the disposal of toxic waste around Corby."

He urged Barron and the council to push for an inquiry with the Cabinet Office.

"Quite literally, local lives depend on it," said Collins.

A spokesperson from the Department of Health and Social Care said: "The government is aware of this issue, and the relevant agencies are monitoring the situation closely to keep the public safe.

"The UK Health Security Agency will continue to provide the necessary support to local authorities, and the Environment Agency will keep the situation under review and will determine whether further action is required."

stories.title: Introducing Our New Surveillance Self-Defense Guide: Online Privacy for Parents and Youth
stories.summary: The internet is a vast and confusing place no matter your age. Trying to help youth engage with it safely and privately is a complicated topic that touches on many different skillsets and ideas. But just because it’s complicated doesn’t mean it’s impossible. We’ve launched our Online Privacy for Parents and Youth Surveillance Self-Defense guide in hopes to provide a framework for finding solutions that work for you. EFF rolls out this crucial resource as state and local governments consider ill-advised laws that cut young people off from essential information and experiences. This particularly harms vulnerable youth and marginalized groups who often find safety in supportive online communities they can't access offline. Such laws also entail age gating, which compromises the privacy of all internet users and stifles young users’ ability to learn, grow , and express themselves . Young people have unique needs and those needs change over time. Trying to protect from everything all the time is an exhausting process, but the security community has long had a solution for this: security planning (also called threat modeling). The idea is to provide a series of questions designed to help you focus on what’s truly important. When it comes to online privacy, this is as applicable for youth and parents as it is for anyone else. We used a security plan as our foundation for this guide because deciding what is and isn’t important is the first step we should all take when assessing our privacy risks. But this isn’t a place for quick fixes, and every young person has their unique needs and considerations. There is no single tool or technology fix that can substitute for spending time learning, and then teaching a young person, how the internet works, how to use it, what sorts of harms exist, and how to navigate those harms. Solutions are rarely about the tools or software you use. It’s about understanding the threats and concerns you have, and then determining what steps you can take to mitigate those risks. We hope our Online Privacy for Parents and Youth guide can help provide the outline to get the conversation started. Donate Today!

stories.title: Interoperability vs. Security: Why not both?
stories.summary: An open internet where people can freely build, share, and remix each other's work is a powerful engine of grassroots innovation we’ve all benefited from. In recent decades, however, corporations have taken control of an increasing share of this work, giving them a greater ability to stifle challengers and limit our choices. When regulators address this by mandating that tech giants play fair by requiring interoperability, the gatekeepers respond with a tired refrain: Playing fair puts users’ security at risk. Unfortunately for these trillion-dollar companies, this gotcha isn’t the end of the conversation. Regulators can ensure that meaningful choice and security thrive. Lawmakers have been catching up, recognizing that the best way to rein in big tech is to require these oligopolies to open up their platforms to independent developers. As we explained six years ago , mandating interoperability helps prevent the misuse of people’s data and enables more privacy-respecting alternatives. Tech giants, in contrast, have been arguing that our data is safer when they have exclusive control. Tech Giants Claim Interoperability Means Insecurity The European Union’s Digital Markets Act (DMA) put interoperability into law under Article 6(7): “gatekeeper shall allow providers of services and providers of hardware, free of charge, effective interoperability with” a designated Core Platform Service they operate. The language describes an unambiguous requirement to remediate vendor lockouts and anti-competitive behavior of the major service operators—it is not optional. Apple claimed that enforcing this obligation in mobile app stores would put their customers at risk and do irreparable harm to trust in their brand. It’s an argument reminiscent of Apple’s fight against the right to repair , and in both instances the company is fighting to maintain its restrictive ecosystem to stop people from finding better deals elsewhere. Apple has long cultivated a more corporate-controlled experience with the iPhone, but this argument is now also being used for the relatively-more-open Android devices from Google. In the same year Apple argued against the DMA, Epic Games sued Google for its restrictive terms of service and extractive policies for revenue generated in apps. stories.title: EFF’s State Legislative Agenda to End ALPR Mass Surveillance
stories.summary: Police agencies across the U.S. have deployed Automated License Plate Readers (ALPRs) to capture images of passing vehicles along with time, date, and GPS coordinates. While the technology itself isn’t new (ALPRs have existed in various forms for more than 50 years , and in the U.S. since 1998 ), the surveillance landscape has shifted dramatically. Rapid advances in artificial intelligence and national data sharing have transformed police ALPRs into an interconnected, nationwide tracking network. It is pitched to city councils by law enforcement and private vendors like Flock Safety, Motorola Solutions (Vigilant), and Axon as an essential tool for solving violent crime. In reality, it is an inherently dangerous infrastructure of mass surveillance. Since 2012 , EFF has worked with others to expose the severe digital rights harms of ALPR systems. For example, we’ve recently documented how these camera networks allow law enforcement to search for immigrants , track peaceful protesters , target Romani communities , and track women seeking reproductive healthcare . Police also routinely use ALPRs for low-level matters like enforcing school residency requirements or investigating noise complaints . Many officers also use ALPR databases to stalk past romantic partners . Recent EFF analysis revealed officers using the system without legitimate justification—logging search reasons like "LOL" and "LMAO." Understandably, the public backlash to police ALPR technology is accelerating, and state lawmakers across the country are taking action. New Hampshire enacted the nation’s first state law on ALPR use in 2007, but technological advances and misconduct have driven even more recent legislative action. In 2026 alone, six states enacted laws that limit police use of ALPRs: Connecticut , Kentucky , New Jersey , New Mexico , Oregon and Washington . This is a good start, but far more is needed. stories.title: EFF Launches Guide to Help Parents and Youth Protect Privacy Online
stories.summary: Guide Includes Easy, Quick Ways To Identify and Protect Against Online Threats SAN FRANCISCO – The Electronic Frontier Foundation (EFF) has published “ Online Privacy for Parents and Youth ,” a new guide to help families protect themselves online. "Parents don’t need to be technology experts to help their children navigate the digital world safely” said EFF Public Interest Technology Director Babette Ngene. “At EFF, we believe in empowering families with the knowledge and confidence to make informed decisions about their digital lives. It’s about meeting families where they are and giving parents the guidance they need to have meaningful conversations with their children about digital safety, based on what works best for their families.” EFF launches this crucial resource as state and local governments consider enacting well-meaning but ill-advised laws that cut young people off from essential information and experiences, particularly harming vulnerable youth and marginalized groups who often find safety in supportive online communities they can't access offline. Such laws also entail age gating, which compromises the privacy of all internet users and stifles young users’ ability to learn, grow, and express themselves. “Deciding how to help your young people use the internet—including engaging with video games, social media, web search, and everything else—is a complicated topic that touches on many different skillsets and ideas,” said EFF Senior Security and Privacy Activist Thorin Klosowski. “But ultimately it's up to families – not governments – to decide when and how to engage with these sorts of questions.” Each young person has unique needs, and, just like their wardrobe, that changes as they age. Parents can engage in thoughtful planning to find the best, most efficient solutions that evolve along with their children. EFF’s guide is about helping parents explore their concerns and identify the threats their children face – like trusting AI chatbots or sharing personal information with strangers – and then determine steps they and their children can take to mitigate those risks while still using the games, educational materials, and communication platforms that help them grow.
